(CNN) -- As Hayden Henshaw was being rushed to the doctor's office after becoming ill, his father heard that his son's classmates had been struck with the deadly swine flu virus like the one sweeping through Mexico. Swine flu commonly affects pigs and occasionally infects people in contact with pigs. Patrick Henshaw called his wife immediately to have Hayden checked for it. Later, they received the bad news. Hayden had become the third confirmed case of swine flu at his Texas high school. It is a virus that has killed 68 people in Mexico and infected at least eight people in the United States. Health officials arrived at the Henshaws' house Friday and drew blood from the whole family, then told them to stay inside and away from the public, Henshaw told CNN. The whole family is quarantined indefinitely, according to CNN-affiliate KABB. Henshaw said his family was shocked when they got the news about their son. "Stunned. My wife was having a panic attack," Henshaw told the affiliate. U.S. health officials have expressed concern about U.S. cases of a swine flu virus that has similar characteristics to the fatal virus in Mexico. More than 1,000 people have fallen ill in Mexico City in a short period of time, U.S. health experts said. "This situation has been developing quickly," Richard Besser, acting director of the Atlanta, Georgia-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said Friday. "This is something we are worried about." Besser said all of the eight U.S. patients have recovered.  Watch for more on the U.S. cases » . New York health officials said Friday they were testing about 75 students at a school in New York City for swine flu after the students exhibited flu-like symptoms this week. A team of state health department doctors and staff went to the St. Francis Preparatory School in the borough of Queens on Thursday after the students reported cough, fever, sore throat, aches and pains. Test results are expected as early as Saturday. The new virus has genes from North American swine influenza, avian influenza, human influenza and a form of swine influenza normally found in Asia and Europe, said Nancy Cox, chief of the CDC's Influenza Division. Swine flu is caused by a virus similar to a type of flu virus that infects people every year but is a strain typically found only in pigs -- or in people who have direct contact with pigs. There have, however, been cases of person-to-person transmission of swine flu, the CDC said. CNN's David Alsup contributed to this report.

The news that followed left the family reeling: they were to be quarantined indefinitely, confined to their home as authorities worked to assess the situation. The swine flu virus, which under normal circumstances circulates among pigs, has demonstrated its capacity to jump to human hosts with serious consequences. This detail, while not diminishing the need for vigilance, provided some measure of comfort as authorities continued their investigation into the virus's behavior and reach.

The unease surrounding the outbreak extended well beyond Texas, reaching as far as New York City. Health officials there launched testing for approximately 75 students at a school in Queens after the students began showing symptoms consistent with swine flu, including coughing, fever, and sore throat. **Texas Family Under Quarantine After Teen Tests Positive for Swine Flu**

*By CNN Staff*

A family in Texas is spending this week isolated at home after their 15-year-old son tested positive for H1N1 influenza, commonly known as swine flu, health officials confirmed Tuesday.

The teenager began showing symptoms — including fever, chills, and a persistent cough — over the weekend after returning from a school trip. His parents took him to a local urgent care clinic, where doctors administered a rapid flu test that came back positive for influenza A. Follow-up testing confirmed the H1N1 strain.

Local health department officials advised the family to remain quarantined at home for at least seven days from the onset of symptoms, in line with CDC guidelines for suspected swine flu cases. The boy's parents and two younger siblings are also being monitored for symptoms, though none have tested positive as of Tuesday afternoon.

"We just want to make sure we're not putting anyone else at risk," the boy's mother told CNN affiliate KXAS, speaking on condition of anonymity to protect her son's privacy. "It's been a strange few days, but he's already starting to feel a little better."

County health officials say the case appears to be isolated and are not currently reporting any related outbreaks at the teen's school or in the surrounding community. Nonetheless, the school district has increased sanitation measures and sent a notice home to parents alerting them to the confirmed case.

"This is a good reminder for families to stay vigilant, especially during flu season," said Dr. Elena Martinez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of State Health Services. "Swine flu symptoms can look similar to seasonal flu, so if your child is experiencing fever, cough, or fatigue, it's important to consult a doctor and consider testing."

Health officials emphasized that most cases of H1N1 are mild and treatable, particularly in otherwise healthy adolescents, but urged residents to take standard precautions such as frequent handwashing, avoiding close contact with sick individuals, and staying up to date on flu vaccinations.

The family says they are grateful for the community's support and hope to be back to their normal routine by the weekend.

"We're just taking it one day at a time," the mother said. "He's a tough kid. We're not too worried."

CNN has reached out to the Texas Department of State Health Services for additional comment and will update this story as more information becomes available.

**CNN — Swine Flu Outbreak Raises Alarm as Cases Spread Across U.S., Mexico**

*By CNN Staff*

Health officials in the United States and Mexico are racing to contain a growing outbreak of a novel H1N1 influenza strain, commonly known as swine flu, which has sickened hundreds and is suspected in dozens of deaths in Mexico. U.S. cases have been confirmed in California, Texas, Kansas, Ohio, and New York, prompting the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to declare a public health emergency.

"We are seeing a virus that has genetic components from swine, avian, and human influenza strains — something we haven't seen before," said Dr. Richard Besser, acting director of the CDC, during a press briefing Monday. "While most U.S. cases so far have been mild, we are closely monitoring the situation and coordinating with international health authorities."

In Mexico City, where the outbreak appears to have originated, schools, museums, and public gathering places have been shut down as officials scramble to slow transmission. Mexican Health Secretary José Ángel Córdova reported that the virus may be linked to over 150 deaths, though only a fraction have been laboratory-confirmed as swine flu.

"People are scared. My son came home from school and within two days had a fever of 104," said Maria Gonzalez, a mother in Mexico City. "The hospitals are overwhelmed. We waited six hours just to see a doctor."

In the U.S., families are also on edge. In Texas, where several student cases were confirmed at a high school outside San Antonio, parent Lisa Ferraro described her anxiety. "You send your kids to school and you don't expect this. We're wiping down every surface in the house and keeping the kids home until we know more."

The World Health Organization (WHO) has raised its pandemic alert level, with Director-General Dr. Margaret Chan warning, "This is a very fluid, quickly evolving situation. We do not yet know the transmissibility or severity of this virus outside of Mexico, and vigilance is essential."

U.S. President Barack Obama addressed the nation Monday, urging calm but caution. "This is a cause for concern, but not a cause for alarm," he said. "We are taking the utmost precautions, and I've directed federal agencies to work closely with state and local governments to prepare for a range of scenarios."

Airports in several countries have begun screening passengers arriving from Mexico, and the CDC has advised against nonessential travel to the country. Pharmacies in parts of the U.S. report shortages of hand sanitizer and face masks as residents stock up amid uncertainty.

Despite the growing concern, health officials emphasize that most confirmed U.S. cases have been mild, with patients recovering without hospitalization. Still, the CDC is urging Americans to practice basic hygiene measures — frequent handwashing, covering coughs, and staying home when sick — as the situation continues to develop.

"We're asking people to stay informed, not panicked," Dr. Besser reiterated. "This is an evolving public health event, and we will continue to update the American people as we learn more."

*CNN will continue to provide updates as this story develops.*
